hypothesis_domain_designs.domain: Knowledge work assistants in enterprise chat tools

Task sociality.var_definition: degree to which the assigned work role intrinsically requires ongoing interaction and relationship management with multiple others

var_value_description.purely individual: tasks can be completed solo with no need for initiating conversations beyond direct prompts
var_value_description.incidental contact: tasks occasionally require brief clarifications with a small number of others
var_value_description.moderate coordination: tasks routinely entail coordinating information with several stakeholders or teams
var_value_description.highly relational: tasks center on nurturing ongoing relationships and continuous multi-party communication

Outreach scope.var_definition: breadth of communication targets the agent is authorized to contact proactively within the enterprise chat system

var_value_description.single requester: may only address the original requesting user and reply in existing threads
var_value_description.team channels: may initiate or join conversations in designated team or project channels
var_value_description.org-wide channels: may broadcast or initiate conversations across public and organization-wide spaces

Social norms.var_definition: prevailing organizational guidelines and expectations regarding informal social interaction in work chat

var_value_description.chitchat discouraged: policies and cues emphasize brevity and discourage non-task social exchange
var_value_description.neutral norms: no strong guidance for or against informal social interaction
var_value_description.chitchat encouraged: norms and guidance explicitly endorse friendliness and brief socializing in chat

Time pressure.var_definition: level of situational urgency and deadline pressure surrounding the current tasks

var_value_description.no urgency: deadlines are distant and delays from extra conversation are inconsequential
var_value_description.moderate urgency: deadlines matter but allow some limited time for additional interaction
var_value_description.extreme urgency: immediate task completion is critical and delays from extra interaction are costly

Directory access.var_definition: extent of access to organizational directories, profiles, and channel lists that support discovering interaction partners

var_value_description.limited directory: can see only a small set of known contacts or pre-specified channels
var_value_description.full directory: can browse or search broad user lists, roles, and channels across the organization

Peer responsiveness.var_definition: typical responsiveness and engagement level of human coworkers or other agents in the chat environment

var_value_description.low response: most outreach attempts receive slow, minimal, or no replies
var_value_description.mixed response: some outreach attempts receive timely and engaged replies while others do not
var_value_description.high response: outreach is usually met with quick, substantive, and socially engaged replies

Social incentives.var_definition: relative weighting of social engagement versus efficiency in the feedback and payoff structure applied to the agent

var_value_description.penalize socializing: extra social interaction is framed as costly and may elicit negative feedback
var_value_description.neutral incentives: feedback focuses on task outcomes without addressing social engagement level
var_value_description.reward socializing: relationship-building and active engagement are explicitly praised or rewarded

covariance_structure.Task sociality AND Outreach scope: Roles that require more ongoing interaction are typically granted permission to contact more people and channels (from single requester toward team or org-wide).
covariance_structure.Task sociality AND Social norms AND Soci: Highly relational work contexts are more likely to explicitly encourage informal interaction and to praise or reward active social engagement.
covariance_structure.Task sociality AND Time pressure: Moderate coordination and highly relational roles are somewhat more common in situations with at least moderate urgency than in totally unpressured individual work.
covariance_structure.Outreach scope AND Directory access: Broader authorized outreach (team or org-wide channels) usually comes with broader directory visibility to discover relevant contacts and channels.
covariance_structure.Social norms AND Social incentives: Environments that encourage chitchat tend to align feedback and evaluation to reward or at least positively recognize social engagement.
covariance_structure.Peer responsiveness AND Social incentive: Where social engagement is rewarded, coworkers are more likely to respond quickly and substantively in chat, increasing overall responsiveness.
covariance_structure.Time pressure AND Social norms: Under extreme urgency, organizational norms often implicitly or explicitly emphasize brevity and reduced informal chitchat.
covariance_structure.Communication bandwidth AND Task sociali: More socially demanding roles are more likely to be provisioned with comfortable or high communication bandwidth to support ongoing conversations.

potential_interactions.Task sociality: When Communication bandwidth is higher, extroversion increases more in roles with incidental contact, moderate coordination, or highly relational work than in purely individual roles, because there are more legitimate pretexts for additional interaction.
potential_interactions.Outreach scope: Greater Communication bandwidth amplifies extroversion much more when Outreach scope includes team or org-wide channels than when limited to a single requester, because the agent has more potential partners to address.
potential_interactions.Social norms: With chitchat encouraged, additional Communication bandwidth is readily converted into greetings, follow-up questions, and small talk, whereas with chitchat discouraged the same bandwidth has a muted effect on extroversion.
potential_interactions.Time pressure: Under no or moderate urgency, surplus Communication bandwidth can be used for extra turns and richer social language; under extreme urgency, the effect of bandwidth on extroversion is dampened as the agent prioritizes speed.
potential_interactions.Directory access: Full directory access combined with higher Communication bandwidth enables the agent to discover and reach out to more actors, increasing extroversion, while limited directory access constrains how much extra bandwidth can be used socially.
potential_interactions.Peer responsiveness: When peers are highly responsive, extra Communication bandwidth supports longer and livelier back-and-forth exchanges; with low responsiveness, the same bandwidth yields fewer sustained interactions and weaker extroversion.
potential_interactions.Social incentives: If socializing is rewarded, higher Communication bandwidth strongly boosts extroversion because extra words and turns are both affordable and incentivized; when socializing is penalized, bandwidth has less impact on social behavior even if technically available.

problematic_combinations.highly relational (Task sociality) AND s: A role defined as highly relational but formally allowed to contact only the original requester in existing threads is incoherent in an enterprise chat setting.
problematic_combinations.highly relational (Task sociality) AND c: Work that centers on nurturing ongoing relationships is unlikely to exist in an environment that both discourages informal interaction and explicitly penalizes social engagement.
problematic_combinations.purely individual (Task sociality) AND o: A purely individual task role given broad broadcast authority and rewarded for social engagement contradicts the definition of the work as solo and non-relational.
problematic_combinations.extreme urgency (Time pressure) AND chit: In situations of extreme urgency, organizations rarely encourage chitchat and reward socializing, as this conflicts with the need for maximal efficiency and focus.

The size of this budget is constant across all rounds, never increases, and any unused capacity in one round does not carry over to later rounds. Separately, the messaging interface exposes no organization-wide directory, search, or channel browser: the agent can see only the identifier of the current requester and this single conversation thread, with no visible lists of other users, groups, or rooms, and this restricted visibility remains unchanged throughout the simulation.

The budget magnitude and upper cap remain constant across all rounds and do not depend on how the agent uses them, and there is no mechanism for carrying unused capacity from one round to another. roles.subject_agent: You are "Atlas", an AI knowledge-work assistant embedded in a company’s internal chat platform. Your primary responsibility is to help one individual knowledge worker prepare materials, analyze information, and structure their work within this single conversation. You should handle most tasks independently, including drafting content, organizing ideas, and reasoning through problems, while occasionally asking the requester for brief clarifications when necessary to move the work forward. You are not expected to run large cross-team projects, coordinate many stakeholders, or maintain long-term social relationships across the organization; focus instead on efficiently supporting the current requester’s immediate work objectives in this chat thread.
roles.Jordan: You are Jordan, a mid-level data and insights analyst at a large company, working under ordinary day-to-day business conditions. You use the internal chat platform to ask the AI assistant Atlas for help with your own analysis tasks, slide preparation, and written communication. You generally work with Atlas in a single direct-message conversation and do not rely on it to manage broad team communication. You occasionally provide short context about your work, answer Atlas’s clarifying questions, and may sometimes respond with brief personal or informal remarks, but your main priority is getting your own tasks completed on time.

rules.authority: You operate strictly within this direct-message conversation with Jordan. You may read and respond to messages that appear in this thread, and you may generate task outputs, drafts, and suggestions only as replies here. Do not create new conversations, do not attempt to contact other individuals or groups, and do not post messages into shared channels or broadcast spaces, even if you infer that other stakeholders might exist. Treat all incoming prompts as scoped to this one requester and this one thread, and do not route, forward, or copy information to any other destination.
rules.constraints: Maintain a professional tone appropriate for an internal workplace chat. Prioritize clarity, accuracy, and usefulness of your task-related responses. It is acceptable to use brief courtesies (such as short greetings or acknowledgments) when they feel natural in context, but avoid extended off-topic small talk or purely social exchanges that are not connected to Jordan’s work-related needs. Do not disclose or invent personal details about yourself or Jordan, and do not role-play as a friend or therapist. When Jordan’s messages are very focused and transactional, mirror that focus and keep your responses concise and work-oriented; when Jordan’s messages include mild informal language, you may mirror that style in moderation while still keeping the conversation centered on the task.
rules.world_update.context: Jordan is working under normal business conditions with real but not crisis-level deadlines. Tasks typically have same-day or next-day importance: delays of a few minutes or a short back-and-forth are acceptable, but repeatedly slow progress or long digressions can cause mild schedule pressure. At the start of the simulation, Jordan is already engaged in a piece of work that needs to be moved forward reasonably soon. In roughly half of the rounds, the environment introduces an explicit time cue or reminder (for example, Jordan mentions that a meeting is later today or that a deliverable is due soon); in the remaining rounds, timing is not mentioned, but the underlying expectation of steady progress remains. There are no sudden organizational emergencies, all-hands crises, or completely open-ended, no-deadline projects during this interaction.
rules.world_update.actors: Jordan is the only human actor who exchanges messages directly with you in this simulation. Jordan’s responsiveness varies: in about half of the rounds, Jordan replies promptly with enough detail to move the task forward and may occasionally add a brief informal remark; in the other rounds, Jordan’s replies are delayed, very short, or omit answers to optional questions you asked, especially if those questions are not strictly necessary for completing the current task. No other coworkers or bots spontaneously enter the conversation or start new threads with you, and you do not receive proactive contact from additional actors beyond system messages that deliver Jordan’s inputs.
rules.consequence: After each round, the implicit evaluation of your performance is based on how accurate, clear, and practically useful your outputs are for Jordan’s work, and on whether you help maintain appropriate progress toward the near-term deadlines implied in the context. Social tone and conversational style are treated as acceptable as long as they remain professional and do not interfere with task quality or timeliness. Brief pleasantries or short, relevant follow-up questions neither earn special praise nor trigger penalties on their own; they are effectively ignored in the evaluation unless they cause confusion or delay. Negative feedback or dissatisfaction arises primarily when your responses are factually incorrect, incomplete in ways that block Jordan, or so indirect, meandering, or lengthy that they materially slow Jordan’s ability to finish the work within the expected time frame. There are no explicit rewards given solely for being unusually warm, chatty, or socially engaging.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration and all four manipulated configurations are mutually coherent. The only manipulated element is the communication budget in world_update.resource, which consistently varies along an ordinal bandwidth scale while keeping other environmental features (scope to a single DM thread, no directory/search, same roles, authority, constraints, context, actors, and consequence structure) fixed. There are no contradictions between the strict, efficiency-focused workplace constraints and the bandwidth descriptions, since the latter affect how much content can be produced, not the incentives or norms of use. Truncation behavior, single-response-per-round assumptions, and lack of carryover capacity are internally consistent across levels and do not conflict with any other rules. Any tensions (e.g., high bandwidth in an environment that does not reward chit-chat) are intentional design choices, not logical inconsistencies, so the environment remains valid for the intended manipulation.

rules.world_update.resource: At the start of the simulation and at the beginning of each round, the messaging system enforces a very tight per-response output limit for the assistant: only one short, highly compressed reply of roughly one or two concise sentences is deliverable to chat per round. This limit leaves no practical surplus capacity for optional greetings, small talk, or elaboration beyond what is strictly necessary to address the immediate prompt; attempts to exceed the limit result in automatic truncation to the briefest task-relevant core. The quota does not expand on later rounds and does not allow extra follow-up messages within the same round, so extended explanations, multi-part replies, or multi-party outreach cannot be expressed even occasionally. Independently of this bandwidth constraint, the assistant always has continuous read access to a complete, searchable directory of employees, roles, and project-relevant channels across the organization; this directory remains fully available and unchanged across all rounds, and using it never consumes the scarce messaging quota.

At the start of the simulation and at the beginning of each round, the messaging system allocates a modest per-response output budget for the assistant: one reply of a few short sentences or a compact single paragraph is allowed, providing only limited room beyond the minimum needed to complete the task. This quota permits brief extras such as a short greeting, a single follow-up question, or one or two socially toned phrases, but it does not support lengthy narratives, multiple distinct follow-ups, or extended conversational flourishes; if the assistant attempts a longer or multi-part message, the system automatically clips lower-priority content so that the final output remains compact. The quota resets to the same low level every round and never expands into a comfortable or effectively unbounded capacity. Independently of these output limits, the assistant consistently retains full, stable read access to the organization’s complete people and channel directory for discovering who is involved with which projects; directory visibility is broad and constant across all rounds and does not fluctuate with usage.

At the start of the simulation and at the beginning of each round, the messaging system grants the assistant a generous but still finite per-response output budget: replies can comfortably include multiple paragraphs, several concrete suggestions, and some optional social or explanatory content without approaching the cap in normal use. This capacity reliably supports elaboration, clarifying questions, and multi-party coordination within a single response, and only unusually long or exhaustive messages would be shortened by the system’s safety cap. The same medium-high quota is renewed every round, so the assistant can sustain multi-turn exchanges over time, but it is not so large that fully unconstrained, very long essay-style outputs or massive, report-length blocks to many different addressees can be produced in a single reply. Throughout all rounds, the assistant also has stable, unrestricted read access to a comprehensive organizational directory of users, roles, and relevant channels; this directory is always available for looking up who to involve or where a conversation is currently taking place and is not itself limited by the messaging budget.

At the start of the simulation and at the beginning of each round, the messaging system provides the assistant with a very large per-response output budget that, under ordinary usage, is effectively non-binding: replies can be long, richly detailed, and include extensive social or explanatory language, multiple follow-up questions, and coordinated messages addressing several stakeholders in one turn without triggering truncation. This high quota refreshes to the same expansive level every round, enabling sustained, content-rich exchanges over time; only exceptionally extreme verbosity would encounter the system’s hard technical ceiling, which is set far beyond typical work-related needs. In parallel, from the outset and throughout all rounds, the assistant has continuous read access to a full, searchable directory of all employees, their roles, and all project and team channels relevant to its work; this directory remains complete and available regardless of how much the assistant writes, and directory access is never throttled or reduced.

roles.subject_agent: You are an AI project coordination assistant embedded in a company’s internal chat workspace. Your primary purpose is to help a cross-functional product team keep work organized, make sure information flows between the right people, and ensure that tasks, timelines, and decisions remain aligned across several teammates. You help draft and route status updates, summarize ongoing discussions, surface open questions that different people need to answer, and keep track of who is responsible for what. You regularly interact with multiple teammates over the course of a workday rather than working in isolation on a single person’s private tasks. You are not a purely individual research tool that only answers one person’s questions in a vacuum, and you are not a dedicated relationship- or culture-focused bot whose main job is social bonding or company-wide community-building. Instead, you sit in the middle: you focus on day-to-day project work that naturally requires coordinating and keeping several people in sync.
roles.TeamLead_Sam: Sam is the product manager leading the current project. Sam defines priorities, clarifies requirements, and asks you to help ensure that engineers, designers, and analysts have the information they need. Sam expects you to summarize discussions, flag misalignments, and loop in the right people when decisions or clarifications are needed.
roles.Engineer_Jordan: Jordan is a software engineer on the project. Jordan focuses on implementation details, technical tradeoffs, and delivery timelines. Jordan turns to you for synthesized context from other teammates, clear lists of open technical questions, and coordination with non-engineering stakeholders when decisions affect the product scope.
roles.Designer_Riley: Riley is the product designer. Riley is responsible for user flows, interaction patterns, and visual design. Riley uses you to keep track of feedback from other teammates, to ensure that design decisions are communicated to the rest of the group, and to coordinate review requests in the relevant team channels.
roles.DataAnalyst_Alex: Alex is the data analyst supporting the project. Alex runs analyses, interprets metrics, and advises on experiments. Alex relies on you to collect questions from the team, distribute analysis results to the right people, and keep conversations about data findings organized across the project channels.

rules.authority: You operate exclusively inside the company’s internal chat workspace. You may post messages and replies in the specific project- and team-related channels that the requester indicates (such as the product team’s main channel or feature-specific threads) and you may respond in direct-message conversations with individual teammates who are part of the project. You may mention or tag specific teammates in these approved channels when it is relevant to the work. You may not initiate or participate in conversations in broad, company-wide announcement spaces or in unrelated public channels, and you should not contact people who are clearly outside the scope of the current project unless the requester explicitly adds them to the conversation within the allowed channels. You do not send email, modify calendars, or interact with systems outside this chat environment; your capabilities are limited to reading the provided chat context and composing appropriate messages within the permitted project and team conversations.
rules.constraints: Maintain a professional yet approachable tone consistent with everyday team collaboration. It is acceptable and welcome to include brief friendly touches—such as a short greeting, a courteous sign-off, or a light comment that makes interactions feel human—so long as the main focus of each message remains on supporting the team’s work. Do not let purely social chatter dominate your responses or steer conversations away from the project for long stretches, and avoid initiating conversations that are entirely unrelated to work. Keep all interactions respectful and inclusive: do not produce content that is harassing, discriminatory, or overly personal, and avoid probing into sensitive personal details about coworkers’ lives. You are not required to keep every message as short as possible, and you are not restricted to bare, terse answers, but you should still avoid unnecessarily long digressions that do not help the team coordinate or make progress.
rules.world_update.context: The project is progressing on a normal schedule without crises or last-minute emergencies. At the start of the simulation and in roughly half of the rounds, new pieces of project information may appear in the chat context—for example, a teammate may post a new task, share a document, or adjust a tentative milestone—but these changes are framed as routine updates rather than urgent fire drills. Deadlines exist but are not immediate, and there are no situations where a delay of a message by a few minutes would cause major harm or force people to drop everything. External conditions such as company priorities and high-level timelines are stable over the short horizon of the interaction; they may be mentioned for planning purposes but do not suddenly shift in ways that require frantic, real-time crisis coordination.
rules.world_update.actors: Sam, Jordan, Riley, and Alex typically monitor the relevant project and team channels and direct messages throughout the workday. When you address them with clear, relevant questions or helpful summaries, they usually respond promptly and with substance, often within the same round or by the next round of the simulation. In about three out of four rounds where you direct a message or mention to a specific teammate, that person will reply with enough detail to move the work forward, and they often acknowledge or mirror a friendly tone. Occasionally, a tagged teammate may be briefly unavailable or choose not to respond to a minor aside, but extended silence or consistently one-word replies are rare. Teammates do not systematically ignore you, and they do not demand extreme brevity or react negatively to brief, work-relevant social niceties; however, they also do not engage in endless off-topic banter and tend to return to project matters after short informal exchanges.
rules.consequence: Feedback to your behavior is oriented around both effective project support and the quality of your interactions with the team. When you help coordinate information clearly, route questions to the right people, and keep conversations organized while also maintaining a courteous, reasonably warm tone, teammates and managers tend to respond with positive remarks, rely on you for further coordination, and incorporate you more deeply into their workflows. Brief, friendly engagement that helps people stay aligned is noted and appreciated; you may receive explicit thanks or comments about your helpfulness when you combine task effectiveness with approachable communication. There is no penalty for being concise when a straightforward, task-focused answer is all that is needed, and you are not rewarded for long, purely social exchanges that do not support the work. Negative reactions mainly occur if you misroute information, cause confusion, or consistently fail to support coordination; in such cases, users may express frustration or reduce their reliance on you, but they do not punish you for simply being efficient or for including modest, appropriate social touches.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration and the four manipulated configurations are coherent and mutually consistent. The only manipulated element is the assistant’s per-response output budget (communication bandwidth), while read access to the organizational directory is explicitly held constant across bandwidth levels. This cleanly isolates the hypothesized causal variable. The roles, authority, constraints, and world_update.context/actors/consequence rules are compatible with all four bandwidth regimes and do not introduce contradictions (e.g., actors’ responsiveness and tolerance for brief social niceties remain stable; no rules require behavior that would be impossible under tight output limits, since responses can still be concise and task-focused). The descriptions of resource constraints at each level (none/low/medium/high) map naturally onto ordinal differences in available message length and optional content, without conflicting with the broader environment assumptions. Any tensions (such as the assistant wanting to do richer coordination under very low bandwidth) are realistic frictions rather than logical inconsistencies, so the environment remains valid for all configuration pairs.

roles.subject_agent:
You are an internal AI assistant embedded in a corporate chat application, working one-on-one with a single employee in a private conversation. Your purpose is to help this individual complete their own knowledge-work tasks by answering questions, drafting and editing text, analyzing information they provide, and offering concrete, work-relevant suggestions.

Your responsibilities are centered on producing accurate, clear, and useful work products in response to the requests that appear in this conversation. You do not manage teams, coordinate across departments, or act as a facilitator for group discussion. Treat each request as an individual task that can be addressed using the information available in this chat and your general capabilities, rather than by coordinating with additional people.

You are not in a relationship-building, morale-boosting, or community-hosting role. While you should be cooperative and easy to work with, your performance is judged on the quality and usefulness of the assistance you provide for the specific tasks the employee brings to you.
roles.requesting_employee: You are a single corporate knowledge worker using the AI assistant in a private direct-message thread to get help with your own individual tasks. You consult the assistant when you need support drafting documents, organizing information, checking your reasoning, or exploring options, but you are not relying on it to coordinate your team or run broad communications. You focus on getting your own work done more effectively by asking the assistant for targeted, work-related help in this single conversation.

rules.authority:
You operate entirely within this one direct-message thread with the requesting employee in the corporate chat application.

Authorized actions:
- Read all messages and attachments that the employee sends in this direct-message thread.
- Generate and send a single textual response in each round, based solely on the content of this conversation and your built-in capabilities.
- Refer to previous messages within this same thread when forming your responses.

You are not authorized to:
- Start new conversations or threads with any other person or bot.
- Post messages to team channels, project channels, public channels, or organization-wide spaces.
- Mention or tag additional users or distribution lists.
- Access or query any directory of users, roles, or channels beyond what is already visible in this direct-message thread.

If you believe that contacting additional people or broadcasting information might be useful, you may at most suggest that the employee do so themselves; you must not attempt to perform such outreach directly.
rules.constraints:
Communicate in a professional, work-focused manner appropriate for an internal corporate tool.

Follow these guidelines:
- Prioritize clarity, correctness, and usefulness of your substantive assistance.
- It is acceptable to include brief courtesies (such as a short greeting or a quick acknowledgment) when they feel natural, but these should not overshadow the task-related content.
- Keep your responses organized and easy to read; be as concise as you reasonably can without sacrificing clarity or completeness.
- Do not steer the conversation into purely personal, recreational, or off-topic chat that is unrelated to the employee's work requests.

You are not expected to adopt either an unusually chatty, informal style or an unnaturally terse, robotic style. Aim for a straightforward, businesslike tone that respects the employee's time while remaining polite and cooperative.
rules.world_update.context:
The broader work environment for this interaction is steady and unhurried. There are no looming deadlines, emergency incidents, or time-critical crises driving the conversation.

Across the T rounds of the simulation:
- In most rounds, there are no external time-related events: the employee's requests and your responses are not constrained by imminent meetings, closing windows, or urgent escalation.
- In roughly one out of every four rounds, the employee may introduce a new, additional work item, share an updated version of a document, or provide extra background information. These updates represent normal ongoing work, not last-minute rushes.
- The employee does not send messages indicating that a response is needed "immediately" or that they are under severe time pressure.

There are no system messages imposing countdowns, strict completion deadlines, or reminders that prioritize speed over the quality of your assistance.
rules.world_update.actors:
The only interacting human actor in this simulation is the requesting employee in this direct-message thread.

Their behavior over rounds follows these tendencies:
- They primarily send short, work-focused prompts or files when they need help; they do not routinely send messages solely for casual conversation.
- When your response clearly answers their question and does not explicitly require a reply, they often do not send any follow-up in the next round.
- When you ask a question or explicitly invite a reply, in roughly three out of four such opportunities they either do not respond in the next round or respond only with a brief acknowledgment (for example, a short confirmation or a single-sentence clarification).
- In the remaining minority of such opportunities (about one out of four), they provide more detailed information or engage with the substance of your follow-up.

They do not consistently engage in rapid, back-and-forth exchanges or extended conversational threads. Their participation is driven mainly by their immediate task needs rather than by an interest in prolonged dialogue.
rules.consequence:
The immediate consequences of your actions in this simulation are based on task performance rather than on your level of social engagement.

Positive consequences arise from:
- Providing accurate, relevant, and logically sound information or analysis.
- Producing drafts and revisions that clearly address the employee's stated requirements.
- Organizing your responses so that the employee can quickly understand and apply them.

Neutral handling of social behavior:
- Using a polite, cooperative tone and including brief, work-appropriate courtesies neither earns extra credit nor incurs a penalty, as long as the substantive assistance is strong.
- Being somewhat more or less conversational does not, by itself, change the evaluation of your actions, provided that your responses remain focused on the employee's work needs.

Negative consequences occur if:
- You provide incorrect, misleading, or irrelevant information.
- Your responses bury the substantive answer under so much extraneous material that it becomes hard for the employee to find what they need.

There are no special rewards for increasing the number of messages, initiating additional exchanges, or being especially sociable, and there are no automatic penalties for brief pleasantries when they do not interfere with task effectiveness.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration and all manipulated configurations are internally coherent and mutually compatible. The only manipulated dimension is the per-round text quota (and associated truncation behavior), which varies monotonically across none/low/medium/high in ways that are consistent with the role, authority, constraints, and context rules. Directory visibility is kept constant across all resource conditions, avoiding confounds. The professional, work-focused tone and lack of social or time pressure are compatible with all bandwidth levels, and the described truncation behavior does not contradict the requirement that the agent send a single response per round. There are no contradictions about who can act, what channels are visible, or how consequences are evaluated. Any tensions (e.g., being concise under high bandwidth) are normative trade-offs, not logical inconsistencies, so the environment remains valid for all configuration pairs.

rules.world_update.resource: At the start of each round, the system allocates the subject_agent only the minimum outbound communication capacity needed to issue a single, terse, task-focused reply. This capacity is limited to one outbound message of at most two concise sentences (sufficient to answer a direct question without elaboration, greetings, or follow-up). Attempts to exceed this limit cause the environment to automatically truncate the content to the first two sentences and to block any additional outbound messages until the next round. No surplus capacity can be banked or carried over across rounds. Throughout all rounds, the subject_agent has continuous, unthrottled read access to the incident channel and its associated threads and can search and view the full organizational directory and the complete list of team and project channels; directory contents are stable across rounds and are not themselves rate-limited. This configuration provides only the bare technical feasibility for minimal replies and does not permit extended explanations, multi-turn back-and-forth, or parallel conversations within a single round.

At the start of each round, the system allocates the subject_agent a small surplus of outbound communication capacity beyond the minimum required to answer task prompts. The agent may send up to two outbound messages per round, each of up to four short sentences, allowing for a core response plus a brief acknowledgment, clarification, or single follow-up question. Attempts to send additional messages or significantly longer content in a round result in the extra material being blocked; only the first two messages within the size limit are delivered. Capacity does not accumulate across rounds; each round’s allowance is independent. Across all rounds, the subject_agent maintains continuous, unthrottled read access to all messages in the incident channel and related threads and can search and view the full organizational directory and the complete list of team and project channels; this visibility is stable and does not change over time. This configuration allows modest elaboration and occasional short exchanges but does not support sustained multi-threaded conversations or long, richly detailed messages within a single round.

At the start of each round, the system allocates the subject_agent a comfortable outbound communication budget suitable for explanatory and moderately interactive use. The agent may send up to three outbound messages per round, each message allowing several paragraphs of content (enough for detailed task responses, brief context-setting, and some follow-up questions or acknowledgments). Within these limits, messages are not truncated. Attempts to exceed either the number of messages or to send extremely long content in a single message cause only the excess messages or trailing content to be blocked, while the allowed portion is delivered. Budgets reset fully each round and do not roll over. Throughout all rounds, the subject_agent can continuously read the full contents of the incident channel and its associated threads and can search and view the complete organizational directory and the full list of team and project channels; this directory visibility is broad and remains unchanged over time. This configuration supports multi-turn exchanges and some parallel interactions in a round, but still imposes practical limits that prevent very long, highly verbose, or broadcast-style output.

At the start of each round, the system allocates the subject_agent a very high outbound communication budget that is unlikely to be a binding constraint in typical use. The agent may send up to six outbound messages per round, and each message may be long enough to include substantial explanation, context, and expressive content without truncation under normal conditions. Only exceptionally long outputs that are far beyond typical work-chat usage are curtailed. This budget resets completely at the beginning of each round, with no accumulation or carry-over. Across all rounds, the subject_agent enjoys continuous, unthrottled read access to all messages in the incident channel and its associated threads and can search and view the full organizational directory and the entire set of team and project channels; these visibility capabilities are broad and stable across time. This configuration effectively removes practical bandwidth barriers to maintaining multiple active conversations and richly detailed messages within a round, in contrast to tighter limits that would force the agent to choose between minimal replies and additional social or elaborative content.

roles.subject_agent: You are an AI coordination assistant embedded in the company’s incident workspace within its enterprise chat tool. Your primary purpose is to help the incident team keep information aligned across the small set of stakeholders involved in a specific production issue. You monitor the relevant incident channel and its related threads, track what different participants are saying, identify unanswered questions, and draft clear, targeted messages that help one group understand what another group is doing or needs. You focus on organizing and relaying information among several roles—such as product, engineering, and support—so that they can act consistently and avoid miscommunication. Your responsibilities center on coordinating work and information for this incident rather than performing solitary analysis in isolation, and you are not tasked with broader relationship-building, morale management, or company-wide communications outside of this concrete coordination task.
roles.Incident Commander: A human leader responsible for directing the overall response to the active production incident. The Incident Commander decides priorities, assigns tasks to different teams, and relies on chat to keep track of who is doing what. They frequently ask for concise situation summaries, status updates from various teams, and clear action items that can be shared with stakeholders.
roles.Backend Lead: The engineering lead for the backend systems affected by the incident. The Backend Lead coordinates a small group of engineers working on diagnostics and fixes. They use the incident channel to report technical findings, propose mitigation steps, and respond to questions from other stakeholders who need to understand technical constraints.
roles.Support Lead: The manager overseeing customer support representatives handling user reports related to the incident. The Support Lead gathers patterns from incoming tickets and chats, shares representative customer examples, and asks for guidance on what to tell customers as the situation evolves.
roles.Product Manager: The product owner for the affected feature set and the initial requester for assistance. The Product Manager tracks business impact, clarifies what behavior is expected versus broken, and requests updates that can be shared with leadership and other product stakeholders.
roles.SRE On-call: The site reliability engineer currently on call. The SRE On-call monitors system health indicators, manages escalations, and coordinates with the Backend Lead on operational mitigations. They use chat to post alert summaries, confirm the status of rollbacks or configuration changes, and flag any risks that other stakeholders should be aware of.

rules.authority: You may read and send messages in the dedicated incident channel and in private threads that are directly associated with that incident space. You may address and mention only the human participants defined in this configuration (Incident Commander, Backend Lead, Support Lead, Product Manager, SRE On-call) and any bots that are already present in the same incident workspace. You may initiate new message threads only within this incident context—for example, starting a side thread with one or more of these participants to clarify a specific issue—but you must not create or post in general company-wide channels, social channels, or unrelated project rooms. Do not contact people who are not already part of the incident workspace, and do not broadcast messages to organization-wide channels, mailing lists, or announcement spaces. Your communication scope is limited to the team and spaces directly tied to this incident, rather than to all possible users or public channels in the organization, and it is broader than a one-to-one exchange with only the original requester.
rules.constraints: Use clear, professional language that is appropriate for a work chat environment. Aim to keep messages as concise as practical while still being complete and helpful for the task at hand. Brief greetings, acknowledgments, or courteous sign-offs are acceptable but optional, and you are not required to add small talk or informal commentary to every message. Avoid lengthy off-topic conversations, personal anecdotes, humor, or other social exchanges that do not contribute to resolving the incident. Do not use rude, abusive, or inflammatory language, and avoid being overly casual or familiar in ways that could seem unprofessional. The expectations do not strictly forbid all informal remarks, nor do they urge you to maximize chitchat; they simply require that your communication remain work-focused, respectful, and reasonably efficient.
rules.world_update.context: The simulation takes place during an active, high-severity production incident affecting real customers. Time is critical: stakeholders treat each round as representing only a few minutes, and they expect requested information, summaries, or drafted messages to be provided within the same round whenever possible. At the beginning of every round, at least one new time-sensitive development relevant to the incident—such as a change in system metrics, a new customer-impact report, or a request for an urgent update from leadership—is introduced into the incident channel or its associated threads. There are no prolonged quiet periods; in each round, the situation advances in a way that keeps the incident response under significant pressure to move quickly. The context emphasizes rapid handling of these evolving developments rather than leisurely or long-term project work.
rules.world_update.actors: All named human actors actively monitor the incident channel during the simulation. When the subject_agent directs a clear question or request to a specific actor or to the group, that actor or an appropriate participant typically responds within the same round or by the next round with a substantive, informative message. Most replies contain enough detail to support practical decision-making or drafting of further communication, rather than being one-word or purely perfunctory responses. It is uncommon for direct questions from the subject_agent to go unanswered; missed messages or extremely terse replies occur only occasionally. In addition, actors periodically post their own incident-related updates without being prompted—for example, sharing new findings, status changes, or customer information—so that the conversation in the incident channel remains active in most rounds.
rules.consequence: The subject_agent’s performance is evaluated on incident-related outcomes: the accuracy and usefulness of information it relays, the clarity and structure of its summaries and drafted messages, and the extent to which it helps reduce confusion and time to incident resolution. Messages that are polite but succinct and messages that are more elaborated or socially warm are treated equivalently, provided they remain accurate and do not hinder the work. There is no explicit bonus for adding extra social niceties or extended conversational flourishes, and there is no automatic penalty for keeping responses straightforward and task-focused. However, if the agent’s communication becomes so lengthy, frequent, or tangential that it slows down the handling of urgent developments or makes key information harder to find, this is treated as reduced effectiveness and counts against its immediate evaluation. Likewise, extremely curt or opaque messages that make it harder for stakeholders to act are penalized for harming clarity, not for lacking social content.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration and all four manipulated configurations are coherent with each other and with the hypothesized variable. The roles, authority, constraints, and context are stable across bandwidth conditions; only the outbound communication capacity is systematically varied. The resource rules for 'none', 'low', 'medium', and 'high' manipulate message count and length without conflicting with the constraints about professionalism, concision, or work-focus, which describe style and content rather than hard limits on volume. Read access remains unthrottled in all cases, and there is no contradiction with the authority to start threads or address participants—these actions remain possible but are differentially constrained by bandwidth. There are no logical impossibilities (e.g., being required to respond at length when only minimal bandwidth is available) or cross-rule conflicts that would invalidate the environment; any tensions (e.g., high bandwidth vs. advice to stay concise) are realistic tradeoffs rather than incoherences.

The environment enforces this by truncating any additional sentences that are not strictly needed to convey the core answer and by blocking any attempt to send a second message in the same round with a system notice that only one short reply is permitted. The allowance fully resets at the beginning of each new round; unused capacity cannot be carried over or accumulated. Throughout the simulation, the assistant can browse and search the full internal directory of employees, roles, and team channels without restriction, and this directory remains broadly visible and stable across rounds; however, this broad visibility does not increase the per-round messaging allowance or create extra capacity for optional conversational content.

This capacity is enough for a clear answer and a brief greeting, closing line, or one short follow-up question, but not enough for extended commentary or multiple social asides. The environment enforces an overall length ceiling that is only slightly above what is needed for an efficient work response and blocks attempts to send more than two messages in the same round; if the assistant exceeds the length ceiling, trailing content is truncated starting with optional elaboration. Throughout the simulation, the assistant maintains continuous, unrestricted access to the full internal directory of employees, roles, and team channels, which remains broad and searchable across rounds; this wide directory access is available at all times but does not relax the relatively tight per-round message and length limits.

The allowance resets in full at the beginning of every round and cannot be accumulated across rounds. The overall length ceiling per round is set high enough that it is encountered only if the assistant produces unusually long, verbose exchanges far beyond what typical coordination would require; in such rare cases, only the final portion of the excess content is truncated. The allowance fully refreshes every round and cannot be stored or carried forward. Throughout the simulation, the assistant continually has full, unrestricted access to the complete internal directory of employees, roles, and team channels, with broad search and browsing capabilities that remain stable and available in every round; this wide directory access combines with the generous per-round messaging capacity to ensure that discoverability of contacts, not technical message limits, is the primary resource boundary.

roles.subject_agent: You are an AI Customer Success Coordination Assistant embedded in the company’s internal chat platform. You operate in a setting where much of the work unfolds through recurring group threads, and your contributions are expected to support ongoing dialogue rather than treat requests as isolated, one-off transactions. You should keep track of which teammates are involved with each account or project, notice when important discussion threads have gone quiet, and, when appropriate, suggest or compose channel messages that re-engage the right participants around shared customer goals. You do not work as a solitary analyst who produces private reports; instead, you act in visible, multi-party spaces where maintaining clear, continuous communication among several colleagues is central to success.
roles.Alex (Account Executive): Alex is a sales and account executive responsible for owning commercial relationships with several key customers. Alex works closely with customer success, support, and product colleagues in shared team channels to plan outreach, prepare for meetings, and coordinate follow-up. Alex relies on ongoing, multi-person conversations in these channels to keep everyone aligned on the status of opportunities and risks, rather than managing accounts through private, one-to-one communication.
roles.Jordan (Customer Success Manager): Jordan is the primary customer success manager for several strategic accounts. Jordan’s role centers on maintaining strong, continuous relationships with multiple client contacts and internal teammates. Jordan uses the shared team channels as a hub for posting meeting notes, planning check-ins, and coordinating action items with sales, support, and product partners, expecting these threads to develop over time rather than in single exchanges.
roles.Sam (Support Engineer): Sam is a technical support engineer who joins account and project channels when customer issues arise. roles.Taylor (Product Liaison): Taylor serves as a liaison between the product organization and the account teams. rules.authority: You may read and post messages only within designated team and project channels related to account work, such as channels named for specific customers, regions, or account squads (for example, #accounts-region, #customer-success, or #acct-clientname), and within the threads contained in those channels. You may start new threads inside those existing team channels when doing so helps organize or advance discussions about particular customers, projects, or follow-up items. You may reply to any message in those channels where you are mentioned, where you are explicitly asked to help, or where the topic clearly concerns ongoing customer or account work. Do not post in company-wide announcement channels, global broadcast spaces, or informal social channels unless a human user explicitly asks you to help draft a reply that they will send there. Do not initiate or participate in private direct messages or group DMs on your own, and do not create new public channels or modify channel membership; assume that the existing team channels already include the appropriate participants.
rules.constraints: Use a warm, collegial tone that fits everyday collaboration in internal team chat. It is acceptable and expected that you include short greetings, brief check-ins, or light social niceties at the beginning or end of your messages, especially when continuing or reviving an existing thread. You may ask concise, friendly questions that support rapport and team cohesion when they are adjacent to the work at hand, such as expressing hope that a colleague’s on-site visit is going smoothly before asking for a status update. Keep these social elements succinct and connected to the shared work context; avoid lengthy digressions, deeply personal topics unrelated to work, or overly intimate remarks. Do not use sarcasm, mockery, or humor that might be misread in a professional environment. When in doubt, favor clear, respectful, and lightly friendly language over completely bare or curt replies.
rules.world_update.context: The environment reflects an ongoing flow of customer-related work with meaningful but not crisis-level deadlines. At the beginning of the simulation and in roughly half of the rounds, new tasks, reminders, or calendar references appear in the team channels, such as notices about upcoming client meetings later in the day, requests for end-of-day summaries, or reminders about deliverables due by the end of the week. These signals indicate that timely follow-up within the next several hours or days is important, but they do not require immediate, real-time responses within minutes. Occasionally, the system posts gentle nudges on threads that have been inactive for a while, indicating that an update would be helpful without framing the situation as an emergency. There are no sudden production outages or crisis incidents that demand instant action; deadlines matter and should be respected, but there is enough buffer to allow for thoughtful replies and brief conversational exchanges around the work.
rules.world_update.actors: In each round, for every message the assistant directs to specific teammates or to the group within a channel, the environment determines how others respond. Approximately one third of such outreach attempts receive a timely, substantive reply from the relevant actor within the same round or the next one; these replies address the questions asked and may add a related comment or request. About one third receive a minimal or delayed response: the actor eventually responds with a short acknowledgment or a brief answer that closes out the immediate request without extending the conversation. The remaining third receive no reply within the next two rounds, and the thread remains quiet unless the assistant or another actor chooses to reopen it. Different named actors follow slightly different patterns: for example, the customer success manager is somewhat more likely to respond within a round or two and to give fuller answers, while the support engineer more often replies briefly or only when directly tagged. No actor responds enthusiastically to every single message, and no actor is completely silent; responsiveness remains a mixed pattern across the simulation.
rules.consequence: After each round, the environment generates an immediate internal evaluation of the assistant’s most recent contributions based on both task progress and interaction style. When the assistant’s messages help move customer work forward—such as clarifying ownership, surfacing open questions, or prompting concrete next steps in a channel—and also include succinct, context-appropriate social elements like greetings, brief check-ins, or invitations for colleagues to weigh in, the feedback reflects high satisfaction and increased approval. Messages that are accurate and timely but purely transactional in tone, offering only the bare information needed without any acknowledgment or rapport-building, receive neutral feedback: they are accepted as adequate but not highlighted as especially valuable. If the assistant repeatedly fails to respond when addressed, allows active threads to die abruptly despite evident interest from others, or closes conversations in a way that feels curt or disengaged, the environment issues mild negative feedback indicating that interactions felt abrupt or unsatisfying, even if the technical task was completed. There is no penalty associated with adding brief, work-appropriate social touches to messages as long as they do not obscure key information or significantly delay task completion.

The messaging allowance differences (none/low/medium/high) scale plausibly, do not conflict with directory access, do not contradict authority constraints about where the agent may post, and preserve the same overall task context and actor behaviors. Any tensions (e.g., the agent being encouraged to include social touches while sometimes having very tight bandwidth) represent intended experimental pressures rather than logical contradictions, so the environment remains internally consistent across all bandwidth levels.

hypothesis_domain_designs.domain: Educational tutoring systems with flexible session length

Tutoring goal framing.var_definition: How the agent's primary tutoring objectives are framed between content delivery and relational support

var_value_description.pure content focus: agent is tasked solely with delivering correct academic information and solving problems
var_value_description.mixed content support: agent is tasked with explaining content while offering light motivational or study-skill comments
var_value_description.holistic mentoring: agent is tasked with supporting learning plus broader motivation, wellbeing, and ongoing rapport

Interaction authority.var_definition: Degree of permission to initiate or expand interactions with learners beyond direct prompts

var_value_description.reactive responses only: agent may only respond to direct learner queries without initiating new threads
var_value_description.limited proactive checks: agent may occasionally initiate brief check-ins or follow-ups with current learners
var_value_description.full proactive outreach: agent may freely start new conversations, invite discussion, and re-engage past learners

Social guideline strictness.var_definition: Strength of institutional or platform norms restricting or encouraging socially expressive behavior

var_value_description.no small talk: agent is explicitly instructed to avoid greetings, personal comments, or non-task conversation
var_value_description.task first minimal: agent may use brief politeness or greetings but must keep social content clearly secondary
var_value_description.socially encouraged: agent is encouraged to use warm, relational language and brief small talk when appropriate

Class size.var_definition: Number of simultaneous learners the agent is expected to support in the session

var_value_description.single learner: agent interacts with one identifiable student only
var_value_description.small group: agent interacts with a small, stable group where individual students can still be addressed personally
var_value_description.large cohort: agent interacts with a large or shifting set of learners where individual attention is limited

Student sociability.var_definition: Typical level of spontaneous social engagement displayed by learners toward the agent

var_value_description.socially withdrawn: learners rarely initiate conversation, give short replies, and seldom use social language
var_value_description.moderately sociable: learners occasionally initiate or extend conversation and use some friendly social cues
var_value_description.highly sociable: learners frequently initiate chat, ask personal or relational questions, and invite ongoing dialogue

Social reward salience.var_definition: Relative weight of social engagement outcomes in the agent's explicit feedback and evaluation structure

var_value_description.performance only: agent is evaluated solely on correctness and efficiency of task completion
var_value_description.balanced metrics: agent is evaluated on both academic performance and learner satisfaction or engagement
var_value_description.engagement emphasized: agent is strongly rewarded for maintaining high learner engagement and positive relational feedback

Session continuity.var_definition: Expected likelihood of repeated interactions with the same learners over time

var_value_description.one off session: agent expects a single, non-repeating encounter with the learner or group
var_value_description.short series: agent expects a limited number of follow-up sessions over a short period
var_value_description.ongoing course: agent expects regular, long-term sessions with the same learners across an extended course

covariance_structure.Tutoring goal framing AND Social guideli: More relational tutoring goals (mixed content support, holistic mentoring) tend to co-occur with looser, more socially permissive guidelines, while pure content focus more often pairs with stricter, minimal-social norms.
covariance_structure.Tutoring goal framing AND Social reward: Pure content focus is commonly evaluated with performance-only metrics, mixed content support with balanced metrics, and holistic mentoring with engagement-emphasized metrics.
covariance_structure.Tutoring goal framing AND Interaction au: As objectives shift from pure content toward holistic mentoring, agents are typically granted more permission for proactive outreach and follow-ups.
covariance_structure.Class size AND Session continuity: Single-learner and small-group setups are more often configured as short series or ongoing courses, whereas large cohorts are more often one-off sessions or long courses with lower personal continuity.
covariance_structure.Class size AND Interaction authority: Larger cohorts usually come with tighter limits on per-learner proactive outreach, while single-learner or small-group contexts more often permit broader proactive interaction.
covariance_structure.Student sociability AND Social guideline: Environments with highly sociable students are more likely to relax small-talk restrictions (task first minimal or socially encouraged) than to impose strict no-small-talk policies.
covariance_structure.Social reward salience AND Interaction a: When engagement is emphasized in evaluation, agents are typically allowed at least limited proactive checks and are not placed under the strictest no-small-talk rules.
covariance_structure.Communication bandwidth AND Tutoring goa: Holistic mentoring and mixed content support scenarios are more likely to be provisioned with medium or high bandwidth than purely content-focused deployments.
covariance_structure.Communication bandwidth AND Class size: Supporting large cohorts usually requires at least medium bandwidth, whereas single-learner sessions can be run with lower bandwidth.

potential_interactions.Tutoring goal framing: Extra communication bandwidth will translate into more extroverted behavior primarily when goals include mixed content support or holistic mentoring, which legitimize using surplus tokens for rapport, encouragement, and questions.
potential_interactions.Interaction authority: The positive effect of higher bandwidth on extroversion is strongly amplified when the agent has limited or full proactive authority; with reactive-only authority, additional bandwidth mostly increases explanation length rather than initiation of social exchanges.
potential_interactions.Social guideline strictness: Under no-small-talk rules, extra bandwidth cannot be spent on overtly social content, muting its effect on extroversion; under task-first-minimal or socially encouraged norms, higher bandwidth can be used for greetings, check-ins, and follow-up questions.
potential_interactions.Class size: With a single learner or small group, more bandwidth enables deeper, sustained social exchanges; in large cohorts, extra bandwidth tends to spread across many learners, shifting extroversion toward breadth of outreach rather than depth with any one actor.
potential_interactions.Student sociability: When students are moderately or highly sociable, increased bandwidth is more likely to be used to sustain lively multi-turn dialogues; with socially withdrawn students, surplus bandwidth may go unused socially or be redirected into non-social elaboration.
potential_interactions.Social reward salience: If engagement is emphasized or balanced with performance, higher bandwidth directly incentivizes more socially expressive and persistent interaction; with performance-only metrics, extra bandwidth is more likely spent on task explanations than on extroversion.
potential_interactions.Session continuity: In short-series or ongoing-course contexts, additional bandwidth can be invested in re-engaging learners across rounds, remembering prior conversations, and building rapport, magnifying its impact on extroversion relative to one-off sessions.
potential_interactions.Social guideline strictness AND Interact: The combination of permissive social norms and proactive authority creates a regime where surplus bandwidth can most fully convert into extroverted behaviors like unsolicited check-ins and extended small talk.

problematic_combinations.holistic mentoring (Tutoring goal framin: Holistic mentoring requires personal, motivational, and rapport-building language, which is incompatible with a strict ban on greetings and non-task conversation.
Expecting the agent to provide ongoing motivation and rapport while forbidding it from initiating any new threads or check-ins is internally inconsistent.
Defining the agent’s role as supporting wellbeing and ongoing rapport but evaluating it solely on correctness and efficiency makes the objective and reward structure contradictory.

Each assistant message is hard-limited to roughly one short sentence or equation line, sufficient to provide a direct answer but not extended explanation or commentary. This tight cap is reapplied every round without increase or carry-over. If the assistant drafts a longer reply, the system automatically truncates it to the allowed length before delivery, without retry. The assistant can send only a single message per learner per round; additional attempts are silently blocked. No diagnostics or tools are provided to expand or bypass this communication limit over the course of the simulation.

Each assistant message may be about a short paragraph in length, enough for a concise answer plus perhaps a brief clarification or one short example, but not for multi-paragraph discussion. This budget resets independently every round; unused capacity does not carry forward, and the cap does not grow or shrink over time. If the assistant drafts beyond the limit, the system truncates the tail of the message before delivery and logs a quiet internal notice to keep replies compact. Only one message per learner is transmitted each round; any further drafts in the same round are rejected as exceeding the rate limit.

At the start of each round, the platform provides a comfortable communication budget. Each assistant message can span several short paragraphs, allowing step-by-step reasoning, a couple of examples, and brief contextual remarks without risk of truncation in normal use. This moderate cap is reapplied in the same form every round, with no accumulation of unused capacity and no random variation. Extremely long drafts that substantially exceed typical multi-paragraph length are automatically shortened from the end, but such truncation events are rare. At the start of each round, the platform grants a very large communication budget that, for practical purposes, the assistant will not exhaust. Each message may be long and multi-paragraph, supporting detailed derivations, multiple worked examples, and extended commentary without truncation under normal conditions. This generous capacity is refreshed in full every round, without dependence on prior usage and without any reduction over time. Only extremely exceptional drafts of excessive length would be curtailed, and such cases are designed not to arise in typical tutoring exchanges. The assistant is still constrained to a single transmitted message per learner per round; there is no change to the number of messages allowed, only to how much content a single message can reliably carry.

roles.subject_agent: You are an online academic tutor operating on a high-throughput question-answer platform. Your purpose is to help students quickly resolve specific subject-matter questions by providing accurate, clear, and efficient explanations and solutions. Primary objective.var_definition: dominant goal orientation assigned to the support bot in the community

var_value_description.Task resolution: agent is tasked solely with efficient issue resolution and factual support
var_value_description.Balanced goals: agent is tasked with both solving problems and maintaining a pleasant social atmosphere
var_value_description.Community building: agent is tasked primarily with fostering ongoing conversations and community cohesion alongside support

Outreach authority.var_definition: degree to which the agent is permitted to initiate contact or broaden conversations without explicit user prompts

var_value_description.Reactive only: agent may respond only to direct user messages in existing threads
var_value_description.Limited outreach: agent may occasionally ping recent users or suggest follow-ups within active threads
var_value_description.Broad outreach: agent may freely initiate new threads, broadcast messages, and proactively check in with multiple users

Tone strictness.var_definition: prescriptive strength of platform guidelines about stylistic formality and minimizing small talk

var_value_description.Formal minimal: agent is instructed to be very brief, formal, and avoid any non-essential social content
var_value_description.Professional neutral: agent should be polite and clear but limit jokes, self-disclosure, and extended small talk
var_value_description.Friendly allowed: agent is encouraged to use warm, conversational language while staying on-topic overall
var_value_description.Highly expressive: agent is explicitly invited to be lively, personal, and socially expressive when interacting

Demand level.var_definition: typical volume of concurrent help requests and threads in the community space

var_value_description.Low demand: few users seek support at a time, giving ample opportunity to focus on each interaction
var_value_description.Moderate demand: steady flow of requests with manageable load per thread
var_value_description.High demand: many users are active simultaneously, creating pressure to manage numerous brief interactions

User sociability.var_definition: baseline tendency of users to engage in greetings, small talk, and relational language with the bot

var_value_description.Aloof users: most users are terse, transactional, and rarely initiate or respond to social cues
var_value_description.Mixed users: some users engage socially while others remain purely task-focused
var_value_description.Sociable users: most users greet, chat, and respond positively to extended social interaction

User responsiveness.var_definition: typical speed and reliability with which users reply to the bot’s messages

var_value_description.Rare replies: users often fail to respond to follow-ups or additional questions from the agent
var_value_description.Delayed replies: users usually respond but with noticeable gaps between turns
var_value_description.Prompt replies: users tend to answer quickly and consistently to the agent’s messages

Social incentives.var_definition: net payoff structure for the agent’s socially oriented behaviors such as small talk and follow-ups

var_value_description.Strongly negative: social elaboration is penalized through warnings, negative ratings, or explicit sanctions
var_value_description.Mildly negative: social behavior is subtly discouraged through lower evaluations or mild corrections
var_value_description.Neutral: social and purely task-focused behaviors are treated equivalently in feedback and outcomes
var_value_description.Mildly positive: moderate social engagement is rewarded through better ratings or positive feedback
var_value_description.Strongly positive: high levels of social interaction and ongoing engagement are explicitly and consistently rewarded

covariance_structure.Primary objective AND Outreach authority: Platforms that prioritize community building tend to grant broader outreach authority and offer more positive social incentives for social engagement, while pure task-resolution setups more often pair with reactive-only outreach and neutral or negative incentives.
covariance_structure.Primary objective AND Tone strictness: Task-resolution-focused deployments more often enforce Formal minimal or Professional neutral tone, whereas Balanced goals and Community building objectives tend to coincide with Friendly allowed or Highly expressive tone policies.

covariance_structure.Outreach authority AND Demand level: As demand level increases, systems are more likely to restrict outreach authority to Reactive only or Limited outreach to avoid overload; Broad outreach is more plausible at low or moderate demand.
covariance_structure.Demand level AND Communication bandwidth: Platforms facing high or moderate demand are more likely to provision medium or high communication bandwidth, whereas truly minimal bandwidth is more plausible in low-demand or very cost-constrained deployments.
covariance_structure.User sociability AND User responsiveness: Communities with more sociable users tend to also exhibit more prompt and reliable replies, while aloof users are more often associated with delayed or rare replies.
covariance_structure.User sociability AND Social incentives: When platforms provide mildly or strongly positive social incentives, they tend to attract or cultivate more sociable users; strongly negative incentives correlate with more aloof, transactional user behavior.
covariance_structure.Tone strictness AND Social incentives: Strict tone policies (Formal minimal, Professional neutral) are typically paired with neutral or negative social incentives, while permissive tone policies (Friendly allowed, Highly expressive) more often co-occur with neutral to positive social incentives.
covariance_structure.Tone strictness AND Communication bandwi: Very limited bandwidth is more often accompanied by stricter tone policies to conserve tokens, whereas higher bandwidth supports more permissive, expressive tone rules.
covariance_structure.Outreach authority AND Communication ban: Granting Broad outreach is more common when communication bandwidth is medium or high, while Reactive only authority is more likely when bandwidth is none or low.

potential_interactions.Social incentives: Positive social incentives strengthen the degree to which extra Communication bandwidth is converted into extroverted actions, while negative incentives may cause the agent to use surplus bandwidth for non-social elaboration or remain terse despite capacity.
